newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Congress to back anyone but Deve Gowda.
newsitem.headline: India's Congress to back anyone but Deve Gowda.

text.p: India's Congress party, riven with sharp divisions over the toppling of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's government last week, offered on Monday to back any new candidate of the ousted coalition for the top job.
"The decision was taken with national interest in mind," Congress spokesman Vithal Gadgil said at the end of a crucial meeting of the Congress Working Committee (CWC).
"The main objective is to contain communal forces and avoid mid-term polls," Gadgil told a news conference.
"The United Front should choose a new leader," he said. "If they change the leader, we will support them and not stake our own claim."

Former Congress minister and CWC member Pranab Mukherjee said the party would withdraw the claim made by party president Sitaram Kesri to form a new government, after the United Front elected a new leader.
Asked how long Congress support to a new government would last, Mukherjee said: "It will depend on their performance."

Deve Gowda, whose government was defeated in a confidence vote on Friday after the Congress withdrew vital support last month, broke a political logjam on Sunday when he told his 15-party coalition that he would meet the Congress demand and step down if his partners so decided.
"G.K. Moopanar fits the bill quite nicely," one Kesri aide told Reuters earlier, referring to the head of caretaker Finance Minister P. Chidambaram's Tamil Maanila Congress.
"Moopanar is a very capabale former Congress leader," he said. "Talks will be held soon. We hope he will agree in the national interest. We must avoid elections at any cost."
Moopanar is a publicity-shy Tamil politician close to Sonia Gandhi, former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi's Italian-born widow who also wields considerable influence with Kesri.
The Congress said earlier on Monday the nation's political crisis could be over in a week as the ousted United Front alliance, for its part, stepped up efforts to find a successor to Deve Gowda.
Until Sunday, Deve Gowda and his partners had steadfastly refused to bow to Congress' stipulation that the coalition change leaders before a new government could be formed.

Deve Gowda's reversal opened the door to a possible new alignment, with the Congress supporting a fresh governing coalition led by the United Front and strongly resembling the centre-left team that fell last week.
It also dramatically reduced the prospects -- at least for now -- of mid-term polls that could benefit Hindu nationalists.
Asked earlier how long it would take the United Front and the Congress to work out a new deal, Gadgil said: "About a week."
The United Front, due to meet on Thursday to choose a new chief, said it had postponed the meeting until April 20.
Deve Gowda's communist allies said their Left Front Bloc would consider pulling out of the alliance if he was replaced as leader.

Apart from Andhra Pradesh state chief minister Chandrababu Naidu, who said he was not interested, Moopanar, Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral and Industry Minister Murasoli Maran, a member of the Tamil group, were reported to be in the fray.
Newspapers said Monday's CWC meeting was shaping up as a battle between Kesri and the party's leader in the lower house, Sharad Pawar, who has given lukewarm support to the move to topple Deve Gowda.
But a party statement after the meeting denied there was a rift.
While the United Front said it was open to forming a fresh coalition under a new leader, it expressed concern over the "credibility" and "durability" of Congress' support.
"That is a matter of negotiation," Gadgil said.

The right-wing Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) scoffed at its rivals' efforts to forge a new government and predicted that a new United Front-led government would last only six months because, like Deve Gowda's coalition, it would fall victim to differences with the Congress.
The BJP is parliament's biggest party with 162 seats in the 542-member lower house. With its allies it controls 193 votes, ahead of the United Front's 178 and Congress's 140.
